activities.title: Plan your fresher week
activities.summary: Balance lectures, reading, rest and campus life in your first week.

content.intro: It's your first week at Akoka. Lectures have started, your roommate wants to go out every evening, and your first assignment is due on Friday.

steps.situation: Monday: you have three lectures and no timetable printed yet. What do you do first?

choices.text: Get the timetable from your department notice board or course rep and write it down
choices.feedback: Good. Knowing where and when lectures hold saves you from missing the first classes.

choices.text: Wait for someone to tell you
choices.feedback: You might miss a lecture or two before anyone remembers to tell you.

choices.text: Skip the first week — nothing happens then
choices.feedback: First lectures often cover course outlines and assessment rules. Don't skip them.

steps.situation: Wednesday evening: your roommate invites you to a hangout at the Lagoon Front, but you haven't started the assignment.

choices.text: Go for an hour, then spend the next evening on the assignment
choices.feedback: Balance. Friends matter, and you've kept time for the work.

choices.text: Stay out late every night this week
choices.feedback: Fun, but Friday will arrive with nothing written.

choices.text: Refuse all invitations for the whole semester
choices.feedback: Your work is safe, but making friends early helps you settle in.

steps.situation: Thursday: you don't understand part of the assignment.

choices.text: Ask the lecturer during office hours or ask classmates in your study group
choices.feedback: Asking early is a strength, not a weakness.

choices.text: Copy a friend's answer
choices.feedback: That's academic dishonesty, and you still won't understand the topic.

choices.text: Guess and hope for the best
choices.feedback: Sometimes it works, but one question could have saved you.

content.debrief: Good planners write down their timetable, keep time for rest and friends, and ask for help early.

activities.title: Security on the campus portal
activities.summary: Make safe decisions about phishing, passwords and user input.

content.intro: You've joined the student team that maintains a (fictional) campus portal.

steps.situation: An email says: 'Your portal account will be deleted today. Log in here to keep it' with a strange link.

choices.text: Don't click. Report it as phishing and warn students through official channels
choices.feedback: Correct. Urgency plus an unknown link is a classic phishing sign.

choices.text: Click to check if it's real
choices.feedback: Opening phishing links can expose your credentials or device.

choices.text: Forward it to every student group
choices.feedback: You'd spread the attack further.

steps.situation: How should the portal store student passwords?

choices.text: As salted hashes with a slow algorithm such as bcrypt
choices.feedback: Right. Even if the database leaks, the passwords aren't readable.

choices.text: Encrypted with one key stored next to the database
choices.feedback: Better than plain text, but whoever gets the key gets every password.

choices.text: In plain text so support staff can read them
choices.feedback: Never. Support should reset passwords, not read them.

steps.situation: The search box puts whatever the user types straight into a database query string.

choices.text: Use parameterised queries and validate the input
choices.feedback: This prevents injection attacks.

choices.text: Hide the search box
choices.feedback: Attackers can still send requests directly.

choices.text: It's fine — students won't try anything
choices.feedback: Assume input can be hostile.

content.debrief: Security habits: verify before you click, hash passwords, and never trust raw input.

Research existing solutions and requirements

activities.title: Design challenge: a lagoon footbridge
activities.summary: Make the key decisions for a pedestrian bridge by the water.

content.intro: Your design team must propose a short pedestrian footbridge over a channel near the (game) lagoon front. Students will cross it every day.

steps.situation: The bridge sits in humid, salty air beside the water. Which material approach do you choose?

choices.text: Steel or reinforced concrete with proper corrosion protection and drainage
choices.feedback: Good: corrosion is the main enemy near salt water, so protection and drainage matter.

choices.text: Untreated mild steel because it's cheapest
choices.feedback: It would corrode quickly and cost more in repairs.

choices.text: Untreated timber
choices.feedback: Untreated timber rots fast in wet conditions.

steps.situation: How do you size the bridge for loads?

choices.text: Design for crowds at peak times plus a safety factor, following the design code
choices.feedback: Correct: crowds after an event are the critical case.

choices.text: Design for one person at a time
choices.feedback: Far too low: crowds will use it.

choices.text: Double the load of a car and skip the code
choices.feedback: Guessing isn't engineering; codes exist for good reasons.

steps.situation: The budget is tight. What do you cut?

choices.text: Simplify the shape and decoration while keeping the safety factors
choices.feedback: Cost savings should never come from safety.

choices.text: Reduce the safety factor
choices.feedback: Never trade safety for cost.

choices.text: Remove the handrails
choices.feedback: Handrails prevent falls into the water.

steps.situation: Before construction, who do you consult?

choices.text: The users, the estate office and accessibility advisers
choices.feedback: Including wheelchair users and the people who will maintain it gives a better design.

choices.text: Nobody — engineers know best
choices.feedback: Designs fail when they ignore their users.

content.debrief: A good design balances safety, durability, cost and the people who will use it.

content.intro: In the (game) campus clinic, a fictional 19-year-old student, 'Tunde', has had a fever and headache for two days. You are shadowing the doctor and are asked what to do next.

steps.situation: Where do you start?

choices.text: Take a history and check the vital signs
choices.feedback: Yes: history and vital signs come before treatment decisions.

choices.text: Give antibiotics straight away
choices.feedback: Treating before assessing risks the wrong treatment.

choices.text: Confirm with a test (a rapid diagnostic test or blood film)

steps.situation: Tunde becomes confused and very drowsy. What now?

choices.text: Recognise a danger sign and escalate urgently to a senior doctor or hospital

choices.text: Wait until tomorrow
choices.feedback: Delays can be dangerous when danger signs appear.

choices.text: Give him a soft drink

activities.title: Proof: √2 is irrational
activities.summary: Order the steps of a classic proof by contradiction.

content.instructions: Arrange the steps of the proof in a logical order.

items.text: Assume √2 = a/b, where a and b are whole numbers with no common factor
Square both sides: 2b² = a²
So a² is even, which means a is even: write a = 2k
Substitute: 2b² = 4k², so b² = 2k², and b is even too
Then a and b share the factor 2, which contradicts the assumption
Therefore √2 cannot be written as a fraction: it is irrational
